---
title: "Method"
subtitle: "Physics-informed features, and an alert rule chosen without looking at the answer"
---

The model here is ordinary — a scikit-learn Isolation Forest, which is the most
common choice made on this dataset. What the project rests on instead is the two
things either side of it: features derived from bearing kinematics rather than
picked off a list, and a lead-time metric built so that it cannot be tuned into a
flattering number.

## Why a bearing defect has a frequency

A rolling-element bearing is a machine with known geometry, so a defect in it does not
produce generic "vibration". Each rolling element strikes the defect once per pass,
and the pass rate follows from the geometry and shaft speed alone. Four rates matter,
one per defect location:

| Frequency | Struck by | Indicates | This rig |
|---|---|---|---|
| BPFO — ball pass frequency, outer race | each ball passing a fixed outer-race point | outer-race spall | 236.403 Hz |
| BPFI — ball pass frequency, inner race | each ball passing a point on the rotating inner race | inner-race spall | 296.930 Hz |
| BSF — ball spin frequency | a defect on a ball itself, once per rotation | rolling-element defect | 139.917 Hz |
| FTF — fundamental train frequency | the cage rotating | cage damage | 14.775 Hz |

Geometry, derivation and provenance are in **[the data documentation](data.qmd)**;
they are properties of the rig, not choices made here.

This is what makes a fault *locatable* rather than merely detectable. Energy rising at
236 Hz and its harmonics says **outer race** — it does not say "something is wrong".
Every feature below exists to make that structure visible to a model that has no idea
what a bearing is.

## The features, and what each is for

**Time domain** — cheap, and the first thing to move:

- **RMS** — total vibration energy. The primary degradation indicator, and on this
  data it rises 11.4× above baseline before Test 3's bearing fails.
- **Kurtosis** — the fourth moment, sensitive to *impulsiveness* rather than
  amplitude. A spall produces sharp repeated impacts, which raise kurtosis while RMS
  is still near baseline, so it can lead RMS. Note this project computes **excess**
  kurtosis, where Gaussian reads 0 and not 3 — every threshold in the bearing
  literature is quoted 3 too high for this column. See [the data
  documentation](data.qmd).
- **Crest factor** and **clearance factor** — peak-to-average shape ratios, the same
  impulsiveness idea normalised differently.

**Frequency domain**, from a Welch power spectral density estimate:

- **Defect-frequency band energy** — power in narrow bands around BPFO, BPFI, BSF and
  their harmonics. This is the physics-informed feature proper: it asks the specific
  question the geometry poses.
- **Spectral entropy** — how evenly energy is spread across the spectrum.
- **High-frequency ratio** — proportion of energy above a cutoff.

## Three feature directions that are the opposite of the intuition

Each of these is a trap that produces a confidently wrong reading, so they are worth
stating plainly — together with how firmly each is actually established here, which
differs between them.

- **Spectral entropy is *higher* in healthy bearings, not lower.** The intuition says
  a fault means disorder means high entropy. The opposite holds: healthy bearing noise
  is broadband and close to flat, which is maximum entropy. A developing defect
  *concentrates* energy into BPFO harmonics — structure, not noise — and structure
  lowers entropy. This one is **pinned by a test**
  (`test_spectral_entropy_faulty_lower_than_healthy`, asserting healthy > faulty on
  synthetic signals), so it cannot silently regress.
- **`high_freq_ratio` runs the other way too**, for the same underlying reason:
  healthy Gaussian noise is already rich in high frequencies, so there is little
  headroom for a fault to add any. Only the `[0, 1]` range is asserted by a test; the
  direction is documented but not pinned.
- **`crest_factor` becomes unreliable at high fault severity.** The standard
  explanation is that it rises early, as discrete impacts appear against a quiet
  floor, then falls back once the defect is severe enough that impacts merge into a
  noise floor the fault itself has lifted — so the peak stops standing out from the
  average. Read monotonically, it will eventually suggest the bearing is recovering.
  Only `crest_factor >= 1` is asserted by a test; the non-monotonicity is a
  documented caution here, not a measurement this project makes.

The uneven footing is deliberate to record rather than paper over: one direction is
enforced by the suite, two are conventions carried from the literature and the feature
definitions. Anything relying on the latter two should re-derive them first.

## The detector

`StandardScaler` → optional PCA → `IsolationForest`, fitted on the **first 60%** of
each series on the assumption that a run-to-failure rig starts healthy, then scoring
the whole series. Isolation Forest suits the problem because it needs no labels and
isolates outliers by random partitioning, which is cheap and explainable.

An autoencoder path exists (PyTorch, optional install) and is handled correctly by the
metric layer, including its inverted sign convention. No autoencoder result is
published: it did not earn a place over the Isolation Forest on this data.

## Turning scores into an alert, without cheating

This is the part that took the work. Three problems have to be solved in order, and
each one is a precondition for the next.

### 1. `is_anomaly` cannot be used at all

`contamination=c` guarantees that fraction of the **training** window is labelled
anomalous, and the training window is the part assumed healthy. Measured: 5.03%, 5.08%
and 8.01% of training files flagged, against configured 0.05, 0.05 and 0.08. So the
label is doing what it was asked to do, and the first flagged file lands at or near
file 0 on every run. The lead time is therefore read from a **score threshold**, never
from `is_anomaly`.

### 2. A single flagged window is not an alert

Runs of consecutive flags occur by chance at those rates — a 10-of-10 rule still fires
at file 9 of Tests 2 and 3. The rule is **k of the last m** files flagged.

### 3. Choosing k and m is where a result gets fabricated

Picking the (k, m) that yields the nicest lead time is precisely the failure the
sustained rule exists to prevent, and it would be invisible in the output. Two things
prevent it here:

**The candidate list is fixed in advance**, ordered by window length then strictness —
3-of-5, 4-of-5, 5-of-5, 6-of-10, … 30-of-30 — and **the first entry that does not fire
on healthy data wins**. That is the *most sensitive* rule meeting the constraint, not
the best-scoring one. Lead time is never consulted during selection.

**The healthy region is split into three disjoint windows**, so no window both sets a
parameter and scores it:

| Window | Slice of the live series | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Calibration | first 10% | sets the score threshold, at a 1% per-file false-alarm rate |
| Selection | 10% – 25% | chooses k and m |
| Held out | 25% – 40% | reports the false-alarm rate — **never touched before this** |

The reported "0 false alarms in 323 / 147 / 949 files" comes from the third window
only, which is what makes it out-of-sample.

The 40% boundary is itself an assumption — a run that degraded early would push the
"healthy" window into the failure and report a real detection as a false positive — so
it is **checked rather than assumed**: `check_healthy_region` verifies RMS stays below
2× baseline throughout. All three runs pass.

### 4. The post-shutdown tail

Each rig auto-terminates on a debris-triggered switch, and the acquisitions after that
read near-zero RMS on every channel. They are not healthy readings, and they must not
anchor a lead time. The tail is **measured per run, not assumed** — 0 files for Test 1,
2 for Test 2, 1 for Test 3 — by requiring *every* bearing to fall below 0.2× baseline,
because one bearing can go quiet through damage but all four go quiet only when the
shaft stops. Test 1 never went quiet at all and ends on its RMS peak, so the usual
"drop the last file" would have discarded the very failure being measured. Details in
[the data documentation](data.qmd).

## What this does not establish

- **Three runs is three samples.** The alert rule is selected per run against that
  run's own healthy data. That is correct procedure, and it is not the same as
  validating a fixed rule on an unseen rig.
- **Zero false alarms is an upper bound.** 147 to 949 held-out files cannot resolve a
  rate below roughly 1 in 1,000.
- **Lead time is anchored on the end of the run.** The rigs ran to destruction, so the
  last live acquisition is taken as the failure — but no independent ground-truth
  failure timestamp exists to check that against, and it ties the number to when the
  rig happened to stop.
- **The defect-frequency features have not been ablated.** Whether they earn their
  place over RMS and kurtosis alone is the obvious next experiment and has not been
  run.
